rv.q: If any Edwardian play has stood the test of time, this is unforgettably it.
It’s an inventive, resonant ending to a timely, memorable revival.
Findlay’s atmospheric take on ‘Rutherford and Son’ is a cult-ish classic by a female playwright finally given the blockbuster production it always deserved.
The long second half is absorbing and its closing moments are startlingly staged.
Still, no evening with Roger Allam and Sam Troughton is wasted, and if you are after a whiff of Chekhov with an English flavour, you could do worse.

Findlay's production provides deeply etched portraits of each character, with the formidable Roger Allam, back at the National for the first time in a decade, in tremendous form as the bewhiskered Rutherford.
Findlay and the cast make it compelling, wringing every ounce of meaning and sense out of each line.
But although this production is worthy, it is not revelatory.

cn.t: Sowerby's 1912 feminist classic receives a powerful if uneven revival, with Roger Allam's commanding central performance and striking production design earning widespread praise despite some finding the staging overly gloomy and the accents impenetrable.
